RAG.explanation: Retrieval Augmented Generation combines search with LLMs to give accurate grounded answers
points: RAG first retrieves relevant documents from a knowledge base using semantic or keyword-based search techniques.
The system then injects the retrieved context directly into the LLM prompt to ground its generation in factual information.
This approach dramatically reduces hallucinations and ensures the model's answers are supported by real retrieved sources.
RAG allows LLMs to answer questions about private documents, up-to-date information, or domain-specific knowledge not present in training data.
Modern production RAG systems frequently incorporate advanced techniques such as re-ranking, query rewriting, and multi-hop retrieval for higher accuracy.

Vector Database.explanation: Vector databases store embeddings and enable lightning-fast semantic similarity search
points: Vector databases use approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) algorithms such as HNSW, IVF, or DiskANN to perform extremely fast similarity searches.
They are optimized to store and query high-dimensional dense vectors (typically 768 to 4096 dimensions) generated by embedding models.
Most vector databases support metadata filtering, hybrid search (vector + keyword), real-time indexing, and upsert operations.
Popular options include Pinecone (fully managed), Weaviate (open-source with hybrid capabilities), Chroma (lightweight and local-first), Qdrant, and Milvus.
They serve as the core retrieval engine in nearly every serious production RAG deployment today.

Chunking.explanation: Chunking splits documents into smaller pieces for efficient storage and relevant retrieval
points: Chunking ensures that documents are broken into sizes that fit within the context limits of embedding models and improve retrieval precision.
Common chunking strategies include fixed-size splitting (e.g., 512 tokens), recursive splitting by paragraphs and sentences, and semantic chunking.
Overlapping chunks (typically 10–30% overlap) help prevent important context from being split across chunk boundaries.
Advanced methods such as parent-child chunking retrieve small precise chunks but return larger surrounding parent context to the LLM.
Effective chunking balances semantic coherence, completeness of information, and avoidance of noisy or redundant retrieval results.

Semantic Search.explanation: Semantic search finds results by meaning not just keyword matching — much smarter
points: Semantic search uses dense vector embeddings to capture the meaning and intent of both queries and documents.
It outperforms traditional keyword search on queries that require understanding synonyms, paraphrases, or conceptual similarity.
The core operation is approximate nearest neighbor search over stored embeddings to find the most semantically similar documents.
Modern semantic search often combines dense retrieval with sparse keyword signals (hybrid search) for best results.
It is the dominant retrieval method in production RAG systems today.

Re-ranking.explanation: Re-ranking re-orders retrieved results to improve relevance before passing them to the LLM
points: Re-ranking applies a more accurate (but slower) model to re-score the top-k retrieved candidates from initial retrieval.
Cross-encoders (which jointly encode query + document) typically deliver the highest re-ranking accuracy.
Popular re-rankers include Cohere Rerank, bge-reranker, and fine-tuned models like monoT5 or flashrank.
Re-ranking significantly improves final answer quality by filtering out false positives from the initial retrieval stage.
It is a standard post-retrieval step in advanced RAG pipelines.

Knowledge Base.explanation: A knowledge base is your collection of documents that RAG searches to answer questions
points: The knowledge base consists of indexed documents (PDFs, web pages, internal wikis, code, etc.) that serve as the factual ground truth.
It is usually stored in a vector database, sometimes combined with keyword indexes for hybrid retrieval.
Quality of the knowledge base directly determines RAG answer accuracy and hallucination rate.
Maintenance includes regular updates, deduplication, cleaning, and metadata enrichment.
Enterprise knowledge bases often include access controls, versioning, and governance features.

Document Loader.explanation: Document loaders parse PDFs, web pages, and files into clean text for RAG pipelines
points: Document loaders extract readable text while preserving structure like headings, paragraphs, and tables where possible.
Popular loaders handle PDFs (PyMuPDF, pdfplumber), web pages (BeautifulSoup, Trafilatura), Word docs, Markdown, and more.
Advanced loaders support OCR for scanned documents and table extraction for structured data.
They often include metadata extraction (source, page number, section title) for better retrieval and citation.
Clean loading is critical — poor parsing leads to noisy chunks and degraded RAG performance.

Query Expansion.explanation: Query expansion rewrites user questions multiple ways to improve search recall and coverage
points: Query expansion generates multiple paraphrases or sub-questions to capture different ways the same intent might be expressed.
It significantly improves recall by retrieving documents that match semantically but not lexically.
Techniques include LLM-based rewriting, HyDE (hypothetical document embeddings), and multi-query generation.
Expanded queries are usually searched in parallel and results are fused or re-ranked.
It is especially effective for complex, ambiguous, or long-tail user questions.

Hybrid Search.explanation: Hybrid search combines keyword and semantic search for better more reliable results
points: Hybrid search fuses sparse (BM25/TF-IDF) keyword matching with dense vector semantic similarity.
It balances lexical precision (exact matches) with semantic recall (meaning-based matches).
Fusion methods include Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), weighted linear combination, or reciprocal score merging.
Most modern vector databases (Weaviate, Pinecone, Qdrant) support native hybrid search.
Hybrid consistently outperforms pure semantic or pure keyword search in production RAG.

Context Window RAG.explanation: RAG stuffs retrieved documents into the LLM's context so it can answer with real knowledge
points: The retrieved documents are concatenated and inserted into the prompt as additional context.
The LLM is instructed to answer only using the provided context to reduce hallucination.
Context window size limits how many chunks can be included (typically 8k–128k tokens in 2025).
Techniques like compression, summarization, or reranking help fit more relevant information.
This is the classic and most widely used RAG pattern in production.

Naive RAG.explanation: Naive RAG indexes documents, retrieves top-k chunks, and feeds them to an LLM without optimization
points: Naive RAG uses simple top-k retrieval based on embedding similarity without any refinement.
It is easy to implement but often suffers from low precision and irrelevant context.
Common issues include poor chunking, no re-ranking, and no query rewriting.
It serves as a strong baseline for measuring improvements from advanced techniques.
Many early RAG prototypes start as naive RAG before optimization.

Advanced RAG.explanation: Advanced RAG adds pre-retrieval and post-retrieval steps to dramatically improve answer quality
points: Pre-retrieval steps include query rewriting, expansion, decomposition, and hypothetical document generation.
Post-retrieval steps include re-ranking, contextual compression, and diversity selection (MMR).
These optimizations significantly boost faithfulness, relevance, and completeness scores.
Advanced RAG often reaches near-human performance on knowledge-intensive tasks.
It is the standard pattern used in production-grade RAG systems today.

Modular RAG.explanation: Modular RAG is a flexible framework where each pipeline component can be swapped independently
points: Modular RAG separates stages (loading, chunking, embedding, retrieval, reranking, generation) as interchangeable modules.
It allows easy experimentation with different chunkers, embedders, retrievers, and LLMs.
Popular frameworks like LangChain, LlamaIndex, and Haystack follow this modular design.
Modularity improves maintainability, testing, and performance tuning.
It enables mixing open-source and proprietary components in the same pipeline.

Agentic RAG.explanation: Agentic RAG uses an AI agent that decides when and how to retrieve information dynamically
points: The agent reasons about whether retrieval is needed and which tool or query to use.
It can perform multi-hop retrieval, reformulate questions, or switch strategies mid-task.
Common patterns include ReAct, plan-and-execute, and self-reflective agents.
Agentic RAG handles complex, open-ended, or multi-step questions better than static RAG.
It often uses function calling/tool use to orchestrate retrieval steps.

Self-RAG.explanation: Self-RAG trains the model to decide when to retrieve and to critique its own generated answers
points: Self-RAG adds reflection tokens so the model critiques retrieval quality and its own draft answers.
The model learns to retrieve only when necessary and to revise incorrect generations.
It reduces unnecessary retrieval calls and improves faithfulness significantly.
Introduced by Asai et al. and shown to outperform standard RAG on many benchmarks.
Requires fine-tuning with reflection data but yields more self-aware responses.

Corrective RAG.explanation: Corrective RAG evaluates retrieved documents and web-searches for more if they are not relevant
points: Corrective RAG adds a retrieval evaluator that scores whether retrieved context is sufficient.
If context is inadequate, it triggers web search, decomposition, or reformulation.
It dynamically corrects weak retrievals to improve overall answer quality.
Particularly effective for questions requiring up-to-date or external knowledge.
Combines local knowledge base with fallback web retrieval when needed.

Sentence-window Retrieval.explanation: Sentence-window retrieval stores small sentences but returns the surrounding context window
points: It embeds and retrieves at sentence level for higher precision.
On retrieval, it expands to return a larger surrounding window (e.g., ±3 sentences).
This provides precise matching while giving the LLM enough context to understand.
Popularized by LlamaIndex and shown to improve RAG quality significantly.
Reduces noise compared to fixed-size chunking while preserving coherence.

Parent-child Chunking.explanation: Parent-child chunking retrieves small child chunks but passes larger parent context to the LLM
points: Small child chunks are embedded for precise retrieval.
On hit, the system returns the larger parent document/section for context.
It balances granularity of search with completeness of information.
Common in LlamaIndex and advanced RAG frameworks.
Greatly improves answer quality on long documents with scattered information.

Recursive Chunking.explanation: Recursive chunking splits text hierarchically using natural boundaries like paragraphs and sentences
points: It tries splitting by paragraphs first, then sentences, then fixed-size if needed.
Respects document structure and preserves semantic coherence.
Widely implemented in LangChain and LlamaIndex as default strategy.
Reduces meaningless splits compared to pure fixed-size chunking.
Often combined with overlap for better context continuity.

Semantic Chunking.explanation: Semantic chunking splits documents at points where the topic meaningfully changes
points: It uses embedding similarity between consecutive sentences to detect topic shifts.
Chunks are created where semantic similarity drops below a threshold.
Produces more coherent and meaningful chunks than rule-based methods.
Popularized by Greg Kamradt and implemented in LlamaIndex.
Improves retrieval relevance and reduces noise in RAG.

Fixed-size Chunking.explanation: Fixed-size chunking splits documents into equal token or character length pieces
points: It divides text into uniform chunks (e.g., 512 tokens or 1000 characters).
Simple and predictable — easy to implement and debug.
Often used with overlap to preserve context across boundaries.
Can create meaningless splits in the middle of sentences or ideas.
Still widely used as a fast baseline before trying advanced strategies.

Overlapping Chunks.explanation: Overlapping chunks share text between adjacent pieces so context is never split abruptly
points: Overlap (typically 10–30%) ensures important information isn't cut in half.
Prevents loss of meaning when a key sentence spans chunk boundaries.
Increases storage slightly but significantly improves retrieval quality.
Standard practice in most production RAG pipelines.
Especially important for narrative text, legal documents, and code.

Sparse Retrieval.explanation: Sparse retrieval uses keyword signals like BM25 to find lexically matching documents
points: Sparse retrieval relies on term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) or BM25 scoring.
It excels at exact keyword matches and entity names.
Very fast and interpretable compared to dense vector search.
Often combined with dense retrieval in hybrid systems for best coverage.
Still widely used as a baseline or complement in RAG pipelines.

Dense Retrieval.explanation: Dense retrieval uses embedding similarity to find semantically relevant documents
points: Dense retrieval embeds both query and documents into high-dimensional vectors.
It captures meaning, synonyms, and intent better than keyword methods.
Requires vector database and ANN index for efficient search.
Dominant in modern RAG for most knowledge-intensive tasks.
Performance heavily depends on quality of the embedding model.

BM25.explanation: BM25 is a classic keyword ranking algorithm that scores documents by term frequency
points: BM25 improves on TF-IDF by adding document length normalization and term saturation.
It remains one of the strongest pure lexical retrieval methods.
Fast and lightweight — no embeddings or neural models required.
Frequently used as the sparse component in hybrid retrieval.
Still beats many dense retrievers on exact-match heavy queries.

FAISS.explanation: FAISS is Meta's fast similarity search library for finding nearest vectors at scale
points: FAISS provides highly optimized ANN indexes (IVF, HNSW, PQ, etc.).
It supports GPU acceleration for extremely fast indexing and search.
Widely used under the hood by many vector databases and RAG frameworks.
Offers trade-offs between speed, memory, and recall.
Essential building block for custom high-performance vector retrieval.

Pinecone.explanation: Pinecone is a managed vector database built for production AI applications
points: Fully managed service with no infrastructure to operate.
Supports real-time indexing, upserts, and metadata filtering.
Native hybrid search and reranking capabilities.
High availability with multi-zone replication.
Popular choice for production RAG at companies like Notion and Shopify.

Weaviate.explanation: Weaviate is an open-source vector database with a built-in hybrid search capability
points: Combines vector search with keyword (BM25) in a single query.
Supports modules for text2vec, image2vec, multi-modal embeddings.
GraphQL API and schema-based data modeling.
Self-hosted or cloud-managed options.
Strong community and integrations with LangChain, LlamaIndex.

Chroma.explanation: Chroma is a lightweight open-source vector database popular for local RAG development
points: Runs in-memory or persistent on disk — no external server needed.
Simple Python API designed for rapid prototyping.
Supports metadata filtering and basic hybrid search.
Ideal for local development, notebooks, and small-scale apps.
Often used in tutorials and early RAG experiments.

Qdrant.explanation: Qdrant is a high-performance vector database with advanced filtering capabilities
points: Written in Rust for speed and efficiency.
Excellent support for payload filtering and complex queries.
On-disk storage with memory-mapped indexes.
Hybrid search and rescoring support.
Popular for both local and production-scale RAG.

Milvus.explanation: Milvus is a scalable open-source vector database designed for enterprise AI workloads
points: Supports billions of vectors with distributed architecture.
Multiple index types (HNSW, IVF, DiskANN) and GPU acceleration.
Time-travel and schema evolution features.
Strong in large-scale recommendation and search use cases.
Backed by Zilliz with managed cloud offering.

LanceDB.explanation: LanceDB is a developer-friendly embedded vector database that runs locally
points: Zero-dependency embedded mode — runs inside Python process.
Native columnar format (Lance) with excellent compression.
Supports SQL-like queries and full-text search.
Great for local RAG, offline apps, and prototyping.
Fast growing adoption in Python data science community.

Embedding Model.explanation: Embedding models convert text into dense numerical vectors that capture semantic meaning
points: Modern embedding models are usually transformer encoders (BERT-style) fine-tuned for similarity.
Popular models include OpenAI text-embedding-3-large, Cohere embed, Voyage, BGE, and E5.
They produce fixed-size vectors (384–4096 dims) optimized for cosine similarity.
Multilingual models support dozens of languages with strong cross-lingual performance.
Embedding quality is often the single biggest factor in RAG retrieval accuracy.

Bi-encoder.explanation: Bi-encoders create independent embeddings for queries and documents for fast retrieval
points: Query and document are encoded separately (two forward passes).
Enables pre-computing document embeddings and fast ANN search.
Most production semantic search uses bi-encoders for scale.
Examples: DPR, ColBERT (late interaction variant), GTE, E5.
Trade-off: slightly lower accuracy than cross-encoders but orders of magnitude faster.

Cross-encoder.explanation: Cross-encoders compare query and document together for highly accurate re-ranking
points: Jointly encodes query + document pair in a single pass.
Produces a direct relevance score — highest precision for re-ranking.
Much slower and cannot be used for first-stage retrieval at scale.
Popular models: monoBERT, Cohere Rerank, bge-reranker.
Standard second-stage reranker in advanced RAG pipelines.

HNSW.explanation: Hierarchical Navigable Small World is a fast graph algorithm for approximate nearest neighbor search
points: HNSW builds a multi-layer navigable graph for logarithmic search time.
Offers excellent speed-recall trade-off for high-dimensional vectors.
Used by default in Weaviate, Qdrant, Pinecone, and many others.
Parameters M and efConstruction control index quality vs build time.
One of the most widely deployed ANN algorithms in production.

ANN Search.explanation: Approximate Nearest Neighbor search trades perfect accuracy for massive speed gains
points: ANN algorithms return approximate top-k results orders of magnitude faster than exact search.
Common methods: HNSW, IVF (inverted file), PQ (product quantization), DiskANN.
Recall@K is typically tuned to 95–99% while achieving 100×+ speedup.
Essential for real-time vector search at scale.
Most vector databases expose tunable precision vs speed parameters.

Cosine Similarity.explanation: Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors to quantify how similar they are
points: Cosine similarity = dot product / (norm_a × norm_b).
It is bounded between -1 and 1, with 1 being identical direction.
Most embedding models are trained to optimize cosine similarity.
It is length-invariant — focuses purely on directional similarity.
Default and most common similarity metric in RAG retrieval.

Dot Product.explanation: Dot product similarity multiplies corresponding embedding dimensions and sums the results
points: Dot product = sum(a_i × b_i) — raw similarity without normalization.
Many models (especially normalized embeddings) use dot product as proxy for cosine.
Faster to compute than cosine (no division by norms).
Used when embeddings are pre-normalized to unit length.
Common in FAISS and many production vector indexes.

L2 Distance.explanation: L2 or Euclidean distance measures the straight-line distance between two embedding vectors
points: L2 distance = sqrt(sum((a_i - b_i)^2)).
Equivalent to cosine when vectors are normalized.
Used when embedding space is not normalized or magnitude matters.
Less common than cosine/dot in modern LLM embeddings.
Still supported by all major vector databases.

Namespace.explanation: Namespaces partition a vector index so different users or tenants have isolated data
points: Namespaces provide logical separation within a single index.
Each namespace has its own set of vectors and metadata.
Enables multi-tenancy without spinning up separate indexes.
Supported natively in Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, and others.
Critical for SaaS applications with per-user or per-tenant data.

Metadata Filtering.explanation: Metadata filtering restricts vector search to documents matching specific tags or fields
points: Filters are applied before or during ANN search to reduce candidate set.
Common filters: source, date, user_id, category, document_type.
Dramatically improves relevance when metadata is rich.
Supported by almost all vector databases with varying query syntax.
Often combined with hybrid search for maximum precision.

Multi-vector Retrieval.explanation: Multi-vector retrieval represents each document with multiple embeddings for better coverage
points: Multiple embeddings per document (e.g., title, summary, sections) increase recall.
ColBERT and multi-vector models store token-level or passage-level embeddings.
Late interaction allows fine-grained matching.
Improves performance on long or heterogeneous documents.
Used in advanced RAG for complex knowledge bases.

ColBERT.explanation: ColBERT stores token-level embeddings per document enabling late interaction for accurate retrieval
points: Late interaction computes query-document similarity after separate encoding.
Produces very high retrieval precision compared to bi-encoders.
Higher storage cost due to token-level vectors.
ColBERTv2 and PLAID improve efficiency.
Excellent for re-ranking and high-precision first-stage retrieval.

HyDE.explanation: HyDE generates a hypothetical document answer and uses that embedding to search for real ones
points: HyDE prompts LLM to write a fake ideal answer to the query.
The hypothetical answer is embedded and used for retrieval.
Often finds better matches than the raw query embedding.
Particularly effective for complex or poorly phrased questions.
Simple yet powerful query rewriting technique.

Query Routing.explanation: Query routing directs different questions to the most appropriate retrieval pipeline
points: Router LLM classifies question type (e.g., history, technical, recent news).
Routes to specialized indexes (vector, keyword, web search, graph).
Improves overall recall and relevance across heterogeneous knowledge.
Common in advanced RAG systems with multiple data sources.
Reduces noise by avoiding irrelevant retrieval paths.

Ensemble Retrieval.explanation: Ensemble retrieval combines results from multiple retrievers and fuses their scores
points: Runs dense, sparse, multi-vector, and other retrievers in parallel.
Fuses rankings using RRF, weighted sum, or learned fusion.
Consistently outperforms any single retriever.
Standard in production-grade RAG pipelines.
Increases robustness across different query types.

Reciprocal Rank Fusion.explanation: RRF combines ranked lists from multiple retrievers into a single better-performing ranked list
points: Assigns score = 1 / (k + rank) for each result.
Sums scores across all retrievers for final ranking.
Parameter-free and surprisingly effective.
One of the strongest fusion methods for ensemble retrieval.
Used by Weaviate, Pinecone hybrid, and many RAG frameworks.

Contextual Compression.explanation: Contextual compression extracts only the most relevant sentences from retrieved documents
points: Uses LLM to summarize or extract relevant parts of each chunk.
Reduces noise and fits more useful context in the window.
Implemented in LangChain and LlamaIndex compressors.
Improves answer quality and reduces token usage.
Trade-off: adds latency from extra LLM calls.

LLM Re-ranker.explanation: An LLM re-ranker scores retrieved passages by asking the model which best answers the query
points: Prompts LLM to rate or rank passages for relevance.
More accurate than cross-encoders in some cases.
Can use chain-of-thought for better judgment.
Expensive but powerful for top candidates.
Used when maximum precision is critical.

Cohere Rerank.explanation: Cohere Rerank is a powerful API for improving search result relevance with a cross-encoder
points: Hosted cross-encoder reranker with multilingual support.
Simple API — pass query and documents, get reranked list.
Often boosts NDCG@10 by 10–30% over initial retrieval.
Optimized for speed and cost in production.
Widely used in enterprise RAG deployments.

Lost in the Middle.explanation: LLMs perform worse on information placed in the middle of long contexts versus edges
points: Research shows best performance when key info is at start or end of context.
Middle sections are often ignored or forgotten.
Mitigated by ordering retrieved chunks strategically (best first/last).
Important when stuffing many documents into long contexts.
Influences chunk ordering and context compression design.

Answer Generation.explanation: Answer generation is the final RAG step where the LLM synthesizes retrieved chunks into a response
points: LLM is prompted with question + retrieved context + instructions.
Common instructions: 'Answer only using provided context', 'cite sources'.
Streaming generation improves perceived latency.
Techniques like CoT or self-reflection improve quality.
Final quality heavily depends on retrieval relevance and prompt design.

Citation Generation.explanation: RAG systems can cite source documents in answers so users can verify the information
points: Model is instructed to add inline citations or footnotes.
References chunk IDs, page numbers, or URLs.
Improves trust and allows fact-checking.
Supported natively in many RAG frameworks.
Critical for enterprise and knowledge-intensive applications.

Grounding.explanation: Grounding anchors LLM responses to retrieved factual sources to reduce hallucination
points: RAG is the most common grounding technique.
Instruction: 'Only use information from the provided context'.
Can include source citation and faithfulness checks.
Alternatives: knowledge graphs, self-RAG, corrective retrieval.
Primary method for trustworthy production LLM applications.

Faithfulness.explanation: Faithfulness measures whether a RAG answer is actually supported by the retrieved documents
points: Compares generated answer against context for unsupported claims.
Automated metrics: RAGAS faithfulness, TruLens groundedness.
LLM-as-judge can score faithfulness effectively.
Critical metric for production RAG quality.
Improves with better retrieval and compression.

Answer Relevance.explanation: Answer relevance measures whether the generated answer actually addresses the question asked
points: Compares question and answer for topical alignment.
Automated via LLM judge or embedding similarity.
Part of RAGAS triad (context relevance + faithfulness + answer relevance).
Catches off-topic or evasive responses.
Improves with strong instruction following.

Context Recall.explanation: Context recall measures whether retrieved chunks contain all information needed to answer
points: Compares ground-truth answer against retrieved context.
Checks if all key facts are present in retrieved chunks.
RAGAS context recall metric is widely used.
Improves with better chunking, query expansion, and multi-vector retrieval.
Directly impacts faithfulness and completeness.

RAGAS.explanation: RAGAS is an evaluation framework that automatically scores RAG pipelines on key quality metrics
points: Measures faithfulness, answer relevance, context precision, and context recall.
Uses LLM-as-judge for reference-free evaluation.
Supports synthetic test data generation.
Widely adopted for offline RAG benchmarking.
Helps compare different chunking, retrieval, and generation strategies.

Trulens.explanation: TruLens is an observability tool for evaluating and debugging RAG and LLM applications
points: Tracks inputs, outputs, context, latency, and cost per call.
Built-in RAGAS-style metrics and custom feedback functions.
Dashboard for comparing experiments and versions.
Integrates with LangChain, LlamaIndex, and raw LLM calls.
Popular for iterative RAG development and production monitoring.

LangSmith.explanation: LangSmith traces, monitors, and evaluates LangChain RAG applications in production
points: Full tracing of chains, agents, and retrieval steps.
Dataset management and evaluation harness.
A/B testing of prompts, models, and retrieval configs.
Production monitoring with alerts and usage analytics.
Official observability platform for LangChain users.

Indexing Pipeline.explanation: The indexing pipeline loads, chunks, embeds, and stores documents for later retrieval
points: Steps: load → clean → chunk → embed → store with metadata.
Must handle various formats: PDF, HTML, Markdown, Word, code.
Metadata enrichment improves filtering and citation.
Incremental indexing supports updates without full re-index.
Critical first half of any RAG system.

Query Pipeline.explanation: The query pipeline takes a user question, retrieves relevant chunks, and generates an answer
points: Typical flow: rewrite query → retrieve → rerank → compress → generate.
Can include routing, multi-query, or agentic logic.
Modular design allows swapping components.
Streaming output improves perceived latency.
End-to-end latency and quality depend on this pipeline.

LangChain.explanation: LangChain is a popular framework for building LLM and RAG applications with composable components
points: Provides chains, agents, retrieval strategies, and memory abstractions.
Huge ecosystem of integrations (vector stores, LLMs, tools).
LangSmith observability tightly integrated.
LCEL (LangChain Expression Language) for composable pipelines.
Widely used for rapid prototyping and production RAG.

LlamaIndex.explanation: LlamaIndex specializes in RAG infrastructure with powerful data connectors and query engines
points: Excellent document loaders and advanced chunking strategies.
Supports multiple indexes (vector, summary, keyword, knowledge graph).
Query engines with routing, sub-question, and recursive retrieval.
Strong focus on advanced RAG techniques and evaluation.
Popular alternative/complement to LangChain for RAG-heavy apps.

Haystack.explanation: Haystack is an open-source framework for building production-grade RAG and search pipelines
points: Modular pipeline design with document stores, retrievers, and generators.
Strong support for Elasticsearch, Weaviate, Pinecone, and others.
Dense passage retrieval and reader models.
Evaluation harness and monitoring built-in.
Popular in enterprise search and RAG deployments.

DSPy.explanation: DSPy automatically optimizes LLM prompts and pipelines using machine learning
points: Treats prompting as programmable and optimizable.
Compilers optimize prompts, few-shot examples, and chain structure.
Significantly improves RAG and agent performance with little manual tuning.
Supports retrieval-augmented chains and multi-stage reasoning.
Emerging as powerful tool for production LLM optimization.

Multi-hop Reasoning.explanation: Multi-hop RAG answers complex questions by chaining multiple retrieval and reasoning steps
points: Breaks complex query into sub-questions.
Retrieves and reasons iteratively.
Handles questions requiring multiple supporting facts.
Implemented via agents or decomposed retrieval.
Greatly improves performance on multi-step QA.

GraphRAG.explanation: GraphRAG builds a knowledge graph from documents enabling complex relational question answering
points: Extracts entities and relationships from text.
Builds graph index for traversal-based retrieval.
Answers global questions better than vector RAG.
Microsoft research project with open-source implementation.
Complements vector RAG for entity-heavy domains.

Long-context RAG.explanation: Long-context RAG passes many retrieved documents into LLMs with very large context windows
points: Leverages 128k–1M+ token context windows (Gemini 1.5, Claude 3).
Reduces need for aggressive compression or chunking.
Can include entire documents or large result sets.
Still limited by quadratic attention cost.
Becoming viable with newer long-context models.

Streaming RAG.explanation: Streaming RAG displays the LLM answer token by token as it generates for faster perceived response
points: Uses streaming inference APIs.
Shows answer progressively as tokens arrive.
Improves user experience on long answers.
Supported by most modern LLM APIs.
Can combine with progressive retrieval.

Conversational RAG.explanation: Conversational RAG maintains chat history so follow-up questions reference previous turns
points: Stores and injects conversation history into context.
Rewrites follow-up questions with history for standalone queries.
Enables multi-turn question answering.
Common in chatbots and assistants.
Requires context management and truncation strategy.

Table RAG.explanation: Table RAG retrieves and reasons over structured tabular data inside documents
points: Extracts and indexes tables separately.
Uses table-specific embedding or linearization.
Handles queries requiring aggregation or lookup.
Tools like LlamaIndex Table QA and Unstructured support.
Important for financial, scientific, and enterprise documents.

Multimodal RAG.explanation: Multimodal RAG retrieves and reasons over images, charts, and text together
points: Embeds images and text in shared space.
Retrieves relevant figures/tables/diagrams.
Multimodal LLMs (GPT-4o, Gemini) reason over mixed content.
Enables visual question answering and chart interpretation.
Growing area with multimodal embeddings and models.

Audio RAG.explanation: Audio RAG transcribes speech then indexes and retrieves from audio content
points: Uses ASR (Whisper) to convert audio to text.
Indexes transcripts for semantic search.
Supports podcast, meeting, lecture search.
Can combine with speaker diarization.
Enables voice-based knowledge access.

Code RAG.explanation: Code RAG retrieves relevant code snippets and documentation to assist with programming tasks
points: Indexes repositories, docs, issues, and discussions.
Supports code-specific chunking and embedding.
Used by GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and dev assistants.
Handles multiple languages and frameworks.
Improves code generation accuracy and relevance.

PDF Parsing.explanation: PDF parsing extracts clean text from PDFs including handling tables, headers, and layouts
points: Tools: PyMuPDF, pdfplumber, PyPDF2, LlamaParse, Unstructured.
Handles layout, tables, images with OCR fallback.
Preserves reading order and structure.
Metadata extraction (title, page, section).
Critical first step for document-heavy RAG.

OCR.explanation: OCR converts images of text like scanned documents into machine-readable searchable text
points: Modern OCR: Tesseract, EasyOCR, PaddleOCR, Google Vision.
Handles printed and handwritten text.
Required for scanned PDFs and images in documents.
Often combined with layout analysis.
Improves accessibility of legacy and scanned content.

Document Hierarchy.explanation: Document hierarchy preserves structure like sections and subsections during indexing
points: Maintains headings, chapters, tables of contents.
Enables section-aware retrieval and citation.
Used in parent-child and hierarchical chunking.
Improves context coherence in answers.
Supported by advanced loaders (Unstructured, LlamaParse).

Chunk Metadata.explanation: Chunk metadata stores source, page number, and section info alongside each embedded piece
points: Enables precise citation and source tracing.
Used for filtering and post-retrieval processing.
Includes document title, author, date, section path.
Critical for faithfulness and user trust.
Standard practice in production RAG.

Retrieval Threshold.explanation: Retrieval threshold sets a minimum similarity score below which chunks are discarded
points: Prevents injecting low-relevance noise into context.
Typically cosine similarity 0.7–0.8.
Dynamic thresholds based on query difficulty.
Reduces hallucinations from irrelevant context.
Common in advanced RAG pipelines.

Top-k Retrieval.explanation: Top-k retrieval fetches the k most similar chunks to the query from the vector database
points: k usually 3–20 depending on context window.
Simple and widely used first-stage retrieval.
Often followed by re-ranking or compression.
Trade-off between recall and context size.
Baseline method in most RAG systems.

Maximal Marginal Relevance.explanation: MMR selects diverse retrieved chunks so the LLM gets broad coverage not just repetitive top hits
points: Balances relevance and diversity in retrieved set.
Uses relevance score minus similarity to already selected items.
Prevents redundant information in context.
Commonly used post-retrieval step.
Improves answer quality on broad questions.

Cache-augmented Generation.explanation: CAG pre-loads the entire knowledge base into LLM context to skip retrieval entirely
points: Stores small knowledge base directly in system prompt.
Eliminates retrieval latency and cost.
Works when knowledge fits in context window.
Used for static or small-domain applications.
Alternative to dynamic RAG for certain use cases.

Knowledge Graph RAG.explanation: KG-RAG traverses structured knowledge graphs to find precise factual answers
points: Extracts entities and relations from documents.
Builds graph for entity-centric retrieval.
Answers complex relational questions better than vector search.
Microsoft GraphRAG and Neo4j integrations popular.
Complements vector RAG for entity-heavy domains.

Step-back Prompting.explanation: Step-back prompting asks a broader question first to retrieve better supporting context
points: Generates a high-level version of the question.
Retrieves context for the broader question.
Uses that context to answer the original detailed question.
Improves retrieval for specific or tricky queries.
Simple yet effective technique.

Decomposed Retrieval.explanation: Decomposed retrieval breaks complex questions into sub-questions and retrieves for each one
points: LLM generates sub-queries from original question.
Retrieves separately for each sub-query.
Aggregates results for final answer.
Handles multi-hop and multi-faceted questions.
Improves coverage on complex topics.

Sparse-Dense Fusion.explanation: Sparse-dense fusion blends BM25 keyword scores with embedding scores for best-of-both retrieval
points: Combines lexical precision with semantic recall.
Uses RRF or weighted fusion to merge rankings.
Consistently outperforms single-method retrieval.
Supported natively in Weaviate, Pinecone, Qdrant.
Standard in production hybrid RAG.

Iterative Retrieval.explanation: Iterative retrieval refines the search query using partial answers from previous retrieval rounds
points: Starts with initial query → retrieve → generate partial answer.
Rewrites query based on gaps in partial answer.
Repeats until sufficient context is retrieved.
Improves recall on complex or underspecified questions.
Used in agentic and corrective RAG patterns.

Adaptive Retrieval.explanation: Adaptive retrieval decides on the fly whether retrieval is needed at all for a given question
points: LLM classifies query as needing retrieval or not.
Skips retrieval for simple or memorized questions.
Reduces latency and cost.
Used in Self-RAG and agentic systems.
Improves efficiency without sacrificing accuracy.

RAG Evaluation.explanation: RAG evaluation measures faithfulness, relevance, and completeness of generated answers
points: Key metrics: faithfulness, context relevance, answer relevance, context recall.
Automated frameworks: RAGAS, TruLens, DeepEval.
Uses LLM-as-judge for reference-free scoring.
Essential for comparing pipeline variations.
Helps catch regressions during development.

Token Budget RAG.explanation: Token budget RAG trims retrieved context to stay within the model's maximum context window
points: Sorts and truncates chunks by relevance score.
Uses compression or summarization to fit more info.
Prioritizes high-quality context within budget.
Critical for models with smaller context windows.
Balances completeness with token constraints.

Hypothetical Document Embedding.explanation: HyDE generates a hypothetical document answer and uses that embedding to search for real ones
points: LLM writes fake ideal answer to the query.
Embeds the hypothetical answer instead of raw query.
Often finds better matches for complex questions.
Simple yet powerful retrieval enhancement.
Widely used in advanced RAG pipelines.

Multi-query Retrieval.explanation: Multi-query generates several paraphrases of the question to increase retrieval coverage
points: LLM creates multiple versions of the query.
Searches each version in parallel.
Merges and deduplicates results.
Improves recall on ambiguous or poorly phrased questions.
Standard technique in LangChain and LlamaIndex.

Fusion Retrieval.explanation: Fusion retrieval merges and deduplicates results from many parallel retrieval strategies
points: Combines dense, sparse, multi-vector, HyDE, etc.
Uses RRF or learned fusion for final ranking.
Consistently achieves top performance.
Used in production systems for maximum coverage.
Handles diverse query types effectively.

Late Chunking.explanation: Late chunking embeds full documents first then chunks the contextualized embeddings for better quality
points: Embeds entire document to capture global context.
Chunks the contextualized embeddings afterward.
Produces higher-quality chunk embeddings.
Improves retrieval relevance significantly.
Popular in recent research and advanced pipelines.

Contextual Retrieval.explanation: Contextual retrieval prepends a document-level summary to each chunk before embedding for better matching
points: Generates short summary for each document.
Prepends summary to every chunk before embedding.
Chunks inherit document-level context.
Improves retrieval on long documents.
Developed by Anthropic and shown to boost performance.

Small-to-Big Retrieval.explanation: Small-to-big retrieves small precise chunks then expands context by returning their parent sections
points: Embeds and retrieves small chunks for precision.
On hit, returns larger parent section or document.
Balances precision and completeness.
Popular in LlamaIndex and advanced RAG.
Great for documents with scattered key information.

Knowledge Distillation RAG.explanation: RAG knowledge distillation trains a compact model on LLM-generated answers to avoid retrieval at inference
points: Uses RAG to generate high-quality answers.
Distills knowledge into smaller student model.
Student model answers without retrieval at inference.
Reduces latency and cost in production.
Maintains high quality with lower compute.

RAG Triad.explanation: The RAG triad evaluates context relevance, groundedness, and answer relevance as three key quality metrics
points: Context relevance: are retrieved chunks relevant?
Groundedness/faithfulness: is answer supported by context?
Answer relevance: does answer address the question?
Used in RAGAS and TruLens frameworks.
Comprehensive automatic evaluation for RAG.
